hints: Focus on the overall shape of melting point across a period, not the exact values. Think where the very high peak and the very low troughs occur.
Notice that the highest peak must be a Group 14 giant covalent element like carbon or silicon, and the lowest points just before C must be a halogen and a noble gas.
Count forward from the noble gas minimum at B. The next element with a slightly higher, low melting point from metallic bonding will be the Group 1 alkali metal.
walkthrough:
**Recall the period trend in melting point**

Melting point is controlled by structure. It rises across metals, peaks at Group 14 giant covalent, then falls sharply to low values for simple molecular non-metals.

Trend: $$\text{metallic (rising) } \rightarrow \text{giant covalent (maximum) } \rightarrow \text{simple molecular (low)}$$

**Identify the landmark points on the graph**

The 6th point is the very highest peak, so it must be a Group 14 element such as $\text{Si}$. The 7th and 8th points drop sharply to low values, so they are Group 15 and 16 simple molecules like $\text{P}$ and $\text{S}$.

**Work backwards to find sodium**

Counting back from $\text{Si}$: point 5 is Group 13, point 4 (D) is Group 12, point 3 (C) is Group 1. Point 2 (B) is the minimum for the Group 18 noble gas, and point 1 (A) is the Group 17 halogen.

So the sequence A to H is $\text{F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S}$, which makes C the alkali metal sodium.

options.A: A is one of the two lowest points at the start. This fits a Group 17 halogen like fluorine with weak van der Waals forces between simple $\text{F}_2$ molecules, not a metallic Group 1 element.
options.B: B is the absolute minimum on the graph. This is characteristic of a Group 18 noble gas like neon with only very weak instantaneous dipole forces between single atoms. Sodium melts higher than this because of metallic bonding.
options.C: C is correct. After the noble gas minimum at B, melting point starts to rise again for the next period. C is low but rising, exactly as expected for sodium with weak metallic bonding ($\text{Na}^+$ in a sea of delocalised electrons), before the rise to magnesium and aluminium and the peak at silicon.
options.D: D is already high up the rising metallic section and levels with the next point. This fits a Group 2 element like magnesium with stronger metallic bonding (2+ ions, more delocalised electrons) than sodium, so its melting point is too high to be sodium.
